Part 1 · The round

Why does an outside operator walk a round, and where does it go?

Part 1 · the plan

From the control room to the drum deck

  1. What only the field seesthe gap between the DCS and the plant
  2. Twelve stationsthe route, station by station
  3. How the scene is builtthe layout file becomes a walkable plant
  4. Moving aroundglide, walk, labels, legend
  5. How long a round takeswalking plus looking

Why walk at all?

The DCS sees transmitters; the field sees the plant

The console shows only what is wired to it.

Local gauges

PI-209, PI-210, PI-220 have no signal: someone must read them.

Hand valves

Eight valves move only by hand; their position is seen, not measured.

Senses

Noise, vibration, heat, smell, drips: no transmitter reports them.

Interactive · walk the round

Twelve stations, 226.6 m there and back

The round follows the flow: tank, strainer, pumps, control valve, preheater, drum.

From layout to scene

The 3-D plant is the Layout tab's file, drawn to scale

Equipment boxes, pipe polylines, valves and gauges come from layout.json.
Readings are live from the simulator; valves are the Field tab's valves.
Teaching layout, assumed: no as-built plant exists.

Interactive · the controls of the 3-D tab

Glide, read, operate, or test yourself

Every arrival is logged: Field round: at station N · name, which the exercises tick from.

Interactive · how long is a round?

Looking takes longer than walking

At 2 min a station the round is about 30 min, so a shift fits two or more.

Part 1 · summary

What part 1 settled

  • The round covers what the DCS cannot see.
  • Twelve stations in flow order, 226.6 m there and back.
  • The scene is the layout file; readings are live.
  • Time goes into looking, not walking.

Part 2 · Local readings

What can only be read in the field, and how is it read right?

Part 2 · the plan

From a dial to a line on the rounds sheet

  1. Three kinds of field readinglocal gauge, local indicator, stem position
  2. Metres of liquidwhy the gauges read in m, and kPa g
  3. Reading a dialrange, divisions, parallax
  4. Where each reading isgrade, deck, tank roof
  5. The rounds sheetwhat counts as a right entry

Interactive · what each reading is

Gauge, local indicator, stem position

Only the three local gauges are field-only; the rest repeat what the console shows, and are a cross-check of it.

Derivation · why gauges read in metres

A pump gauge in metres reads head

Pump curves are in metres of head, so the gauges are too.

$h$
head: height of a column of the liquid
m
$\rho$
gas oil density (model)
870 kg/m³
$g$
gravity
9.81 m/s²
$p$
gauge pressure
kPa g
$$p=\frac{\rho\,g\,h}{1000}\qquad 1\ \text{m}=\frac{870\times 9.81}{1000}=8.53\ \text{kPa}$$

Interactive · read the dial, then convert

Read to the nearest small division

Previous slide$p=\rho\,g\,h/1000$

A small division is 3.5 m on the wide dial and 1.5 m on the narrow one: read between the marks.

Interactive · readings by level

Most readings are at grade; one needs a climb

The LT-200 roof indicator is read from the ground on the round; climbing the tank needs a permit.

Interactive · is my entry right?

A reading is right within its tolerance

Accepted if $|a-t|\le\max(\text{tol},\,0.02\,|t|)$, against the plant when Check is pressed.

Part 2 · summary

What part 2 settled

  • Three gauges are field-only; indicators cross-check the DCS.
  • Gauges read head: 1 m of gas oil = 8.53 kPa.
  • Read between the marks; enter within tolerance.
  • Entries are checked against the plant at Check time.

From the valve register to a line-up check

  1. The valve registernormal position and purpose of each valve
  2. The normal line-upset it, check it

Interactive · twelve valves on the round

Normally open, normally closed, sealed, check

The 3-D tab refuses a sealed or locked valve: moving it needs a permit and the seal register.

Interactive · set the normal line-up

Both pumps ready, vents and drain shut

Spare lined up: suction and discharge open, so it can start at once.

Interactive · how fast does a valve move?

A gate valve takes 25 s; a vent 2 s

The line-up says where a valve should be; moving it there takes time.

The model moves a gate 4 % per second and a vent or drain 50 % per second, as the Field tab.

Interactive · read, operate, look

Each close-up writes one line to the event log

Every field action leaves a trace the exercises can read.

The log lines are what the exercises check: read it, check it, or operate it in the field.

Interactive · identification at station 5

Name every item before you touch one

The tab's target is 90 % over every station tried; wrong boxes show the right tag only after grading.

Part 3 · summary

What part 3 settled

  • Twelve valves: five NO, three NC, two sealed or locked, two check.
  • Normal line-up: both pumps ready, vents and drain shut.
  • A hand-wheel takes 25 s from open to shut.
  • Identify first; every read, check and move is logged.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Walk the round in flow order; look at every station.

2

Read local gauges in metres; convert with $\rho g$.

3

Record readings; report changes, do not explain them in the field.

4

Know each valve's normal position before moving it.

5

Never move a sealed or locked valve without a permit.
